03 – The CausalCCC tutorial with default parameters (case study 1)

Does the published code, run as in the tutorial, reproduce Figure 2?

Author

Minh Le, Jeanne Leclerc

Published

October 11, 2026

Goal

Notebook 02 showed that MIIC gives exactly the authors’ network when it is run on the authors’ three input files. Here we build those input files ourselves, from the public data, by following the CausalCCC tutorial with its default parameters, then run MIIC with the settings of the authors’ server job and compare the network with theirs and with the statements of the paper (Results, case study 1, of Dupuis et al., Nucleic Acids Research 2025, doi:10.1093/nar/gkaf404).

Inputs: the NicheNet Seurat object (data/case1/nichenet_seurat/), and the authors’ server job (data/case1/causalccc_server_eaP9Br0llvzxN07zZZEC/) for its L-R pairs and for the comparison. Outputs in results/case1/03_tutorial_default_params/: the CausalCCC input files (causalccc_files/, the files the web server accepts), the MI tables (MI_tables/), the MIIC result (miic_input/), and two files reused by notebook 04 (t_cells.rds, gene_aliases.tsv).

Running time

The gene selection takes about 10 minutes per cell type and MIIC about 15 to 30 minutes. Both results are saved the first time and reloaded afterwards. To force a new run, delete selected_genes.rds or miic_input/miic_result.rds.

Setup

miic must be loaded before causalCCC: the gene selection calls miic() without importing it. The shared helper functions are in scripts/helpers.R (all case studies) and scripts/case1/case1_helpers.R (this notebook and the next one).

library(tidyverse)
library(Seurat)
library(miic)
library(causalCCC)

find_repo_root <- function(dir = getwd()) {
  while (!(file.exists(file.path(dir, "README.md")) && dir.exists(file.path(dir, "notebooks")))) {
    parent <- dirname(dir)
    if (parent == dir) stop("Repository root not found. Open the repository folder in Positron.")
    dir <- parent
  }
  dir
}

root        <- find_repo_root()
source(file.path(root, "scripts", "helpers.R"))
source(file.path(root, "scripts", "case1", "case1_helpers.R"))

authors_dir <- file.path(root, "data", "case1", "causalccc_server_eaP9Br0llvzxN07zZZEC")
results_dir <- file.path(root, "results", "case1", "03_tutorial_default_params")
dir.create(results_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

Fix for SeuratObject 5. causalCCC.MIselection() and causalCCC.mosaic() read the counts with GetAssayData(slot = "counts"). Since SeuratObject 5.3 the slot argument is an error (it was replaced by layer). patch_causalccc() makes copies of the two functions with layer instead, for this R session only.

patch_causalccc()

1. The cells

The Seurat object was made with Seurat v3 in 2019, so it is updated first. We keep the CD4⁺ T cells (senders) and the CD8⁺ T cells (receivers), from both conditions (steady state and 72 h after LCMV infection), as the authors did.

seurat_obj <- UpdateSeuratObject(readRDS(file.path(root, "data", "case1", "nichenet_seurat", "seuratObj.rds")))
t_cells    <- subset(seurat_obj, subset = celltype %in% c(senders, receivers))
rm(seurat_obj)

table(t_cells$celltype, t_cells$aggregate)   # SS = steady state, LCMV = after infection
       
        LCMV   SS
  CD4 T 1961  601
  CD8 T 1252  393
saveRDS(t_cells, file.path(results_dir, "t_cells.rds"))

Same counts as the authors? For each of the 144 variables of the authors’ input, we look for the gene of our object whose counts, in the cells of the same type, are exactly the authors’ values (compared as sorted values, because the authors’ table has no cell names).

matched <- match_authors_genes(t_cells, authors_dir)

matched |>
  count(found_with = case_when(is.na(object_gene)   ~ "no gene with these counts",
                               object_gene == gene  ~ "same name",
                               .default             = "another name"))
# A tibble: 2 × 2
  found_with       n
  <chr>        <int>
1 another name     7
2 same name      137
# The genes found under another name
renamed <- matched |> filter(object_gene != gene) |> distinct(authors_name = gene, object_name = object_gene)
renamed
# A tibble: 4 × 2
  authors_name object_name
  <chr>        <chr>      
1 Mir703       mmu-mir-703
2 Rack1        Gnb2l1     
3 Ifi209       Pyhin1     
4 Tpt1-ps3     Gm14456    
write_tsv(renamed, file.path(results_dir, "gene_aliases.tsv"))
aliases <- setNames(renamed$authors_name, renamed$object_name)   # our name = authors' name

Every variable of the authors’ input is found in our cells with identical counts. Four genes (seven variables, as some are measured on both sides) carry a different name in the authors’ table, because their count matrix used a newer gene annotation (for example, Rack1 is the current name of Gnb2l1). From now on we translate our names into theirs when comparing.

2. The ligand–receptor pairs

Case study 1 uses L-R pairs inferred by NicheNet. We take the authors’ 18 pairs from their server job and remove the _senders / _receivers suffixes; causalCCC.mosaic() adds them again where needed. (The tutorial’s own function for L-R pairs, causalCCC.links(), uses LIANA and currently fails for mouse data inside OmnipathR.)

interact_edges <- read_tsv(file.path(authors_dir, "clean_interact_edges.tsv"),
                           col_names = c("ligands", "receptors"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), strip_suffix)) |>
  distinct()

3. Build the CausalCCC input with the default parameters

build_causalccc_input() (in scripts/case1/case1_helpers.R) runs the tutorial steps:

  1. causalCCC.MIselection(): for each cell type, the genes sharing the most mutual information (MI) with the ligands (CD4⁺) or with the receptors (CD8⁺). With the default n_genes, it keeps 4 genes per gene of interest, i.e. 40 for the 10 ligands and 32 for the 8 receptors, plus the 3 best genes of each gene of interest;
  2. causalCCC.mosaic(): the mosaic table, one row per cell, NA outside each cell type’s genes;
  3. causalCCC.state_order() and causalCCC.layout(): the variable descriptions and the drawing layout.
default_settings <- list(remove_ribo = FALSE, n_genes = NULL, sender_genes_in_receivers = FALSE)
built <- build_causalccc_input(t_cells, interact_edges, default_settings, results_dir)

Number of variables of each group in the new input:

count(built$state_order, group)
            group  n
1         ligands 10
2 receivers genes 44
3       receptors  8
4   senders genes 50

The genes ranked by MI with the genes of interest, as drawn by causalCCC.MIselection():

knitr::include_graphics(file.path(results_dir, "MI_tables", paste0(c(senders, receivers), "_MI_heatmap_filtered.png")))

4. Run MIIC with the authors’ settings

The four files in causalccc_files/ can be uploaded to the web server. Instead, we run MIIC locally with scripts/run_miic.R, which uses the settings of the authors’ server job (notebook 02, section 2), in particular the confidence filter (100 shuffles, ratio 0.01) and the strict orientation threshold (0.01). The server’s default settings are different, so a network from the server with its default settings could not be compared fairly with the authors’.

miic_result <- run_miic_authors_settings(built, results_dir, root)
attr(miic_result, "run_time")
Time difference of 10.55179 mins

5. Compare with the authors

We read both networks in the same format: one node per gene and side (B2m(S) in sender cells, B2m(R) in receiver cells), our gene names translated into the authors’. The authors’ network is the one of their January 2025 run (edgesList.miic.summary.txt_save, notebook 02).

authors_nodes <- read_nodes(read_tsv(file.path(authors_dir, "clean_state_order.tsv"), show_col_types = FALSE))
authors_net   <- read_network(read_tsv(file.path(authors_dir, "edgesList.miic.summary.txt_save"),
                                       show_col_types = FALSE), authors_nodes)

our_nodes <- read_nodes(built$state_order, aliases)
our_net   <- read_network(miic_result$all.edges.summary, our_nodes)

Genes.

6. The links described in the paper

The paper describes 17 links of Figure 2 (paper_links in case1_helpers.R). For each, the table gives its orientation in each network, or “absent”.

check_paper_links(list(authors = authors_net, ours = our_net)) |>

What we learned

The data are the authors’. Our CD4⁺ and CD8⁺ T cells (2,562 and 1,645, both conditions pooled) have exactly the counts of the authors’ input, for all 144 variables; four genes only carry newer names in their table.

The tutorial with default parameters does not reproduce the authors’ input. It selects 112 genes (60 sender, 52 receiver), of which only 61 are among the authors’ 144, and 33 are ribosomal protein genes, none of which the authors kept.

Hence a different network. With the authors’ MIIC settings, our network has 282 links and contains 107 of the authors’ 364 (92 with the same orientation). Of the 17 links described in the paper, 12 are found. Three of the 5 missing ones involve receiver genes that the default selection does not keep (Cd8b1, Ly6c1); the other two (H2-K1 – Shisa5, H2-D1 – Mir703) are between genes present in our input, so the other selected genes changed the network around them. The central statement, Stat1 → B2m as a genuine cause, holds. Stat1 – Isg20 is oriented Stat1 → Isg20 here, bidirected in the authors’ network.

Since MIIC is reproducible (notebook 02), these differences come from the gene selection. Notebook 04 looks for the settings that explain them.
